subject: anatomy
title: Tracheobronchial Tree, Bronchial Circulation, and Inhalation Dynamics

steps.tx: The respiratory tree receives an essential dual vascular supply fulfilling distinct physiological duties: the high-volume low-pressure pulmonary circulation dedicated to alveolar gas exchange, and the systemic **bronchial arteries** dedicated to high-pressure nutritional perfusion of the lung parenchyma, tracheobronchial walls, pulmonary vascular adventitia, and visceral pleura.
steps.say: The lungs possess a dual circulation: the pulmonary vessels for alveolar gas exchange, and the bronchial arteries for nourishing the airways, vessel walls, and visceral pleura.

vis.alt: Diagrammatic comparison of pulmonary gas exchange circulation and high-pressure bronchial systemic circulation
vis.caption: Dual vascular architecture contrasting low-pressure pulmonary and systemic bronchial circulations. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The origin of the bronchial arteries differs symmetrically: the left side receives two bronchial arteries directly from the anterior aspect of the descending thoracic aorta, whereas the right side typically receives a single **right bronchial artery** originating from the third posterior intercostal artery or upper left bronchial artery.
steps.say: Bronchial artery origins are asymmetric: the left lung receives two arteries directly from the descending thoracic aorta, while the right lung receives one artery usually arising from the third posterior intercostal artery.

rows: Right into azygos; left into hemiazygos

steps.tx: In chronic cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis, aspergilloma, or advanced bronchiectasis, chronically inflamed bronchial arteries become markedly hypertrophied, tortuous, and fragile under systemic arterial pressures. Spontaneous rupture of these high-pressure vessels into bronchial lumina produces life-threatening massive **hemoptysis**, requiring emergency transcatheter bronchial artery embolization to arrest endobronchial exsanguination.
steps.say: In tuberculosis or bronchiectasis, bronchial arteries hypertrophy under systemic pressure. Rupture into the airways causes massive hemoptysis, managed by urgent transcatheter bronchial artery embolization.

steps.tx: The trachea bifurcates into primary bronchi at the level of the sternal angle (T4/T5), marked internally by the cartilaginous keel termed the carina. The **right main bronchus** is wider, shorter (2.5 cm long), and courses more vertically (at an angle of twenty-five degrees) than the left main bronchus.
steps.say: The trachea divides at the carina into primary bronchi. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and courses more vertically than the left main bronchus.

vis.alt: Gross anatomy of trachea, carina, right main bronchus, and left main bronchus
vis.caption: Tracheobronchial bifurcation illustrating the wider, more vertical orientation of the right main bronchus. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Because the right main bronchus is wider and more in direct line with the tracheal lumen, **foreign body aspiration** in toddlers occurs predominantly into the right bronchial tree. In a supine patient, the aspirated object characteristically lodges in the superior (apical) bronchopulmonary segment of the right lower lobe, which projects directly posterior.
steps.say: Because the right bronchus is wider and steeper, aspirated foreign bodies enter the right lung far more often. In a supine patient, objects lodge in the apical segment of the right lower lobe, which opens straight backward.

left.title: Right Main Bronchus
points: More vertical course (25 degrees from vertical)
Common destination of aspirated foreign objects

right.title: Left Main Bronchus
points: More horizontal course (45 degrees from vertical)
Rare site of initial foreign body lodgment

steps.tx: Lymphatic drainage of lung parenchyma follows deep peribronchial lymphatics to the bronchopulmonary (hilar) lymph nodes, which drain sequentially into the superior and inferior **tracheobronchial lymph nodes** around the carina. Enlargement of subcarinal nodes from metastatic bronchogenic carcinoma splays the carina, widening its normal acute bifurcation angle.
steps.say: Pulmonary lymph flows to hilar nodes, then ascends to tracheobronchial nodes around the carina. Metastatic subcarinal lymphadenopathy splays the carina, widening its bifurcation angle on bronchoscopy.

steps.tx: The inferior border of the lung root extends downward from the hilum toward the diaphragm as a bilaminar fold of mediastinal pleura designated the **pulmonary ligament**. This pleural sleeve provides vital dead space to accommodate expansion of pulmonary veins during times of increased cardiac output during vigorous exertion.
steps.say: Below the hilum, mediastinal pleura descends toward the diaphragm as the pulmonary ligament. This fold provides anatomical dead space that accommodates pulmonary venous distension during exertion.

right.title: Pulmonary Ligament (Below)
points: Double vertical pleural fold devoid of cartilage
Contains loose areolar tissue and lymphatics
Dead space allows inferior vein dilatation

steps.tx: Parasympathetic innervation of the tracheobronchial tree is derived from the **vagus nerve**, mediating bronchoconstriction, pulmonary vasodilation, and secretomotor stimulation to mucous glands. Sympathetic fibers from T2-T5 thoracic ganglia mediate bronchodilation and vasoconstriction, providing the pharmacological rationale for beta-2 agonist bronchodilators in asthma.
steps.say: The vagus nerve supplies parasympathetic fibers causing bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion. Sympathetic fibers produce bronchodilation, underpinning the action of beta-2 agonists in asthma.
